lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan 4856-CN of US$96 million for the Second Guangdong Pearl River Delta Urban Environment Project (P081776), approved 21 March 2007 and effective 27 June 2007. The revised amount and the disbursed amount were both US$70.92 million. Closing moved from 31 December 2012 to 31 December 2013, with a restructuring on 7 November 2012. Environmental category A. Total project cost was US$187.90 million at appraisal and US$147.13 million actual. The implementing agencies were the Guangdong World Bank Financed Projects Management Office and the provincial Department of Finance, with project implementation units in Foshan and Jiangmen. There were no co-financiers. The completion report of 25 June 2014 rated outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate; the Independent Evaluation Group's review posted 9 February 2015 agreed on every one of those four ratings (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR3107, 25 June 2014; IEG ICR Review ICRR14568, posted 9 February 2015).

companies.name: Hohai University
companies.role: Prepared the resettlement planning for the project and then acted as the external resettlement monitoring institution for the Foshan component, producing six external monitoring reports on the Fenjiang River north bank rehabilitation and five on the Zhen'an wastewater treatment plant. The same body wrote the plan and monitored its implementation (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 June 2014).

companies.name: Chancheng District Government
companies.role: The district-level government of Chancheng District, Foshan, within Guangdong province. The completion report records it as the body that coordinated and negotiated with affected people and entities and ran the mechanism for collecting their views (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 June 2014).

fenjiang-river-foshan-resettlement.community: The project built wastewater collection and treatment, sludge disposal, sediment removal and flood protection works in Foshan and Jiangmen. Two of the four Foshan subcomponents took land and homes. The Fenjiang River north bank comprehensive rehabilitation permanently took 85.22 mu of state-owned land and 1.68 mu of collective land, relocated 15 households with 46 people including two vulnerable people, and demolished 59,790.56 square metres of buildings, of which 2,676.39 square metres belonged to the 15 households. Fifty-three local enterprises and shops were partly affected. The resettlement plan had provided for 10 households and 38 people; the completion report gives 15 households and 46 people as the outcome. A note under the report's own comparison table says the number of relocated households changed "mainly due to family spliting after parents passed away", although the note says reduced where the table shows a rise from 10 to 15. The third phase of the Zhen'an wastewater treatment plant took 86.89 mu of state-owned land against 45 mu in the plan, because a further 41.89 mu was added for a future fourth phase of the plant, and demolished 43,324.17 square metres of enterprise buildings, of which 19,201 square metres was for that future phase; it affected 8 local enterprises, 2 owners and 16 contractors, and 256 people. Total buildings demolished rose from 105,442.04 square metres planned to 112,084.73 square metres. The count of affected people fell from 1,974 in the plan to 302, which the report attributes to no enterprise or shop being wholly relocated and to two of four vulnerable people having died. The report records some delays in carrying out resettlement actions and states that apart from those there were no other issues related to land acquisition or resettlement of affected people. It states that all assets were compensated under contracts signed before the assets were taken, at rates not lower than the plan, that the rate for demolishing the 15 private houses rose about 140 per cent, that the sampled households and enterprises received full replacement cost, and that every affected household and enterprise received 100 per cent of its compensation when the contract was signed. The external monitor reported that none of the 46 people in the 15 households changed livelihoods and that all were relocated and compensated for house demolition. The monitoring institute recorded not a single complaint or grievance during implementation. The same report gives two different counts of industrial closures in the project area and does not reconcile them: the results section says 144 industrial enterprises were shut down or relocated during the project period, and an annex says 34 enterprises were closed or relocated out of the Foshan urban area. Both figures describe municipal pollution-control action rather than works the loan financed.
fenjiang-river-foshan-resettlement.displaced_label: households relocated, from the World Bank completion report's resettlement annex
fenjiang-river-foshan-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,980 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The nearest figure in the Bank's own documents is 1,974, the number of affected people estimated in the resettlement action plan; the completion report puts the actual number affected at 302. The count of people actually relocated in the same report is 46, in 15 households.
fenjiang-river-foshan-resettlement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2013 after a one-year extension. Resettlement was recorded as complete, with compensation paid in full before assets were taken and no grievances logged. In February 2014 the Foshan project management office sent the Bank a summary report of resettlement implementation prepared by the external monitoring institution, and compliance with the resettlement policy was found satisfactory. The Jiangmen component involved no resettlement.

The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of this resettlement was found; searches in Chinese for the Foshan works returned only World Bank material. The documents record the losses and also record that they were paid for: compensation at or above planned rates, full replacement cost on the sampled cases, payment before assets were taken, no complaints, and no change of livelihood among the 46 people moved. The 15 households and 46 people are the outcome figures in the report's own plan-against-actual table, not the plan's figures. The report names no affected person, gives no date for any relocation, and does not say where the 15 households went. The 144 and 34 enterprise-closure figures in the same report are not reconciled and both refer to municipal action rather than the loan's works.
fenjiang-river-foshan-resettlement.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment and on involuntary resettlement. An environmental impact assessment and environmental management plan were reviewed and disclosed before approval, and the management plan was disclosed on 29 April 2006. A resettlement action plan was prepared for the Foshan component and disclosed on 27 April 2006; implementation began in 2006 and was completed by loan closing. A supplemental environmental management plan was prepared and disclosed when the sludge treatment component was redesigned. Environmental management measures were written into the bidding and contract documents. The plan carried grievance and redress procedures under Chinese law and Bank policy, which were disseminated among the affected groups. Resettlement implementation was reported in semi-annual progress reports and monitored externally by Hohai University, which had also written the plan (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 25 June 2014; IEG ICR Review, posted 9 February 2015).

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-80010 of US$100 million for the Zhejiang Qiantang River Basin Small Town Environment Project (P116656), approved 20 January 2011 and effective 6 May 2011, with US$85.69 million disbursed. The revised amount stayed at US$100 million. The project was restructured on 10 March 2015 and closed on 31 December 2016, its original closing date. Total project cost was US$215 million. Environmental category A. The implementing agency was the Zhejiang Provincial Construction Commission Project Management Office. There were no co-financiers. The completion report of 7 June 2017 rated outcome Highly Satisfactory, Bank performance Highly Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Moderate; the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00003951, 7 June 2017; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 11 November 2017).

companies.name: Hohai University
companies.role: Monitored implementation of the resettlement action plans for the project and produced the periodical monitoring reports the completion report relies on (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2017).

companies.name: Zhejiang Provincial Construction Commission Project Management Office
companies.role: The project management office of the construction commission of Zhejiang province, the provincial department responsible for urban and rural construction; it was the project's implementing agency, working through county-level project management offices and project implementation units (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2017).

qiantang-small-town-house-demolition.community: The project built water treatment plants and distribution networks, wastewater collection networks and treatment plants, storm water networks, associated roads, river embankment works and the Qingshankejiawu landfill at Meicheng town in Jiande, across eight counties and districts and 24 towns, townships and communities in four municipalities of Zhejiang. The completion report's resettlement annex gives the outcome against the plan. Permanent land acquisition came to 98.73 hectares and affected 513 households and 1,731 people, against 611 households and 2,084 people planned. Houses were demolished over 26,606 square metres, affecting 73 households and 281 people, against 203 households and 730 people planned, a drop of 47 per cent in area which the report attributes to a revised utility design in Tonglu and to a dropped civil works contract in Pan'an. Temporary land use came to 95.89 hectares and affected 789 households and 2,827 people. The largest house demolition was at Meicheng in Jiande, 35 households and 145 people, where the landfill was built; the report lists among the project's resettlement experiences the protection of households in the buffer zone of the landfill and the wastewater treatment plant in Jiande by relocating and resettling them. Demolition also took place at Jiande, 14 households and 46 people, Shenze in Jinhua, 3 households and 9 people, Qujiang, 1 household and 5 people, and Longyou, 20 households and 76 people. Relocation increased in Jiande and Qujiang because households in the buffer zones of the landfill and the Qujiang wastewater treatment plant were added, and in Longyou because urban planning changed to fit the expanding urban area. The total number of people affected by land acquisition and resettlement was 4,839, 14 per cent fewer than planned. The final resettlement cost was RMB 142 million, about US$20.88 million, 15.5 per cent below the plan's budget. The report states that compensation standards for land acquisition and house demolition were not lower than those in the plans, that all compensation was paid before relocation and before the impacts occurred, that all 1,207 eligible affected people were identified and placed in the national social security programme, and that the external monitor and Bank supervision found the affected people had restored their standard of living and were generally satisfied. At Qujiang the project acquired the affected houses but let the households stay until the last moment before demolition.
qiantang-small-town-house-demolition.displaced_label: households whose houses were demolished, from the World Bank completion report's resettlement annex
qiantang-small-town-house-demolition.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,379 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The appraisal document expected 183 households with 650 people to be affected by the demolition of their houses; the completion report's outcome column gives 73 households and 281 people. The report's total of people affected by land acquisition and resettlement of any kind is 4,839.
qiantang-small-town-house-demolition.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2016 on its original date. The completion report records the resettlement as satisfactorily implemented and the house demolition as 47 per cent below the planned area. The Independent Evaluation Group's review reports the same 26,606 square metres and states that compensation was paid to affected people in a timely manner. The review also reports the final resettlement cost as 141,998.7 RMB against an original estimate of 167,009.9 RMB, dropping the thousands unit the completion report's table carries; the completion report's figures are RMB 141,998,700 and RMB 167,009,900.

qiantang-small-town-house-demolition.conditions: The project was environmental category A. Besides environmental assessment, three safeguard policies were triggered: physical cultural resources, because four old bridges in the project areas were identified as physical cultural resources; involuntary resettlement; and safety of dams, because some of the water supply systems the project built drew directly from reservoirs held by existing dams, although the project financed no dam. Environmental assessments and environmental management plans were prepared and disclosed at appraisal, emergency preparedness plans were prepared for the dam safety policy, and a supplemental environmental management plan was prepared and disclosed in 2014 for subprojects added at restructuring. Resettlement plans were prepared and publicly disclosed at appraisal. The affected people took part in investigating, recording and evaluating the impacts, resettlement schemes were agreed with each affected household, and compensation standards were set no lower than the plans. Implementation of the plans was monitored by Hohai University (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2017; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 11 November 2017; Project Appraisal Document, 12 December 2010).

laibin-water-environment-displacement.title: 416 Families Moved for Laibin's Flood and Drainage Works
laibin-water-environment-displacement.place: Laibin city, on the Hongshui and Beizhijiang rivers and the Caoxiegou stream, Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China
laibin-water-environment-displacement.point: Laibin city, the project area, which the completion report describes as the main urban area of the much larger Laibin prefecture (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Laibin)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-82490 of US$80 million for the Guangxi Laibin Water Environment Project (P126817), approved 31 May 2013 and effective 8 November 2013. The loan was cut to US$66 million by a cancellation of US$14 million and US$62,756,145 was disbursed. Closing moved from 31 January 2019 to 31 January 2020 after a 12-month extension. Total project cost fell from US$127.38 million at approval to US$114.94 million actual, with the borrower's share rising from US$47.38 million to US$52.18 million because of additional land acquisition and resettlement costs. The project was restructured on 19 June 2017 and 15 January 2019. There were no co-financiers. The completion report of 22 June 2020 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial. The World Bank declared misprocurement on a contract that was not substantially complete at the closing date (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR00004961, 22 June 2020; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 17 December 2020).

companies.name: Laibin Municipal Government
companies.role: The municipal government of Laibin, a prefecture-level city of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. It was responsible for the counterpart funds that paid compensation, and the completion report records that delays in mobilising those funds followed the higher land acquisition and resettlement costs. Its project management office and project implementation units ran the works and the grievance mechanism (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2020).

laibin-water-environment-displacement.community: The project was named for the water environment but what it built was flood control and urban drainage: embankment and river works on the Hongshui and Beizhijiang rivers and the Caoxiegou stream, and sewage and storm drainage networks in the old urban area of Laibin city. It acquired 48.02 hectares of land, 15.35 hectares state-owned and 32.67 hectares collectively owned rural land, about 64 per cent of it cultivated. Acquiring the state-owned land affected 11 enterprises and demolished 63,953 square metres of structures, the great majority of them vacant workshops. The land acquisition in the rural areas economically displaced 215 households with 1,075 people and physically displaced 416 families with 2,363 people, demolishing 87,500 square metres of residential housing. The resettlement action plan had provided for the demolition of 36,097.3 square metres of rural residential houses affecting 93 households and 339 people. The outcome was therefore about four and a half times the planned number of households and seven times the planned number of people, and about 2.4 times the planned area of housing. Planned permanent land acquisition was 359.31 mu and the actual figure was 720.35 mu. The actual resettlement cost was RMB 172.66 million, about US$24.88 million, more than three times the appraisal estimate of RMB 54.65 million; the completion report attributes that partly to the increased volume and partly to new local compensation standards set in 2017 for land acquisition, building replacement cost and other compensation. The report states that resettlement funds were paid to affected people on time from the annual fiscal budget, that affected land and property were surveyed and valued with the effective participation of the affected people, that the project gave replacement apartments with tenure security instead of cash compensation, and that vocational training, small credit and social pensions were provided. It records that no complaint was logged through the grievance mechanism during implementation and that there were no outstanding grievances at closing, and says the affected people did not use the mechanism because land acquisition and resettlement issues were resolved through public participation and consultation. The external monitoring agency concluded that the land acquisition and relocation were legally completed and that the objectives of the resettlement plans were materially achieved. The completion report's own lesson from the project is to estimate land and resettlement complexity and cost realistically in rapidly urbanising areas, noting that the costs here were more than three times the appraisal estimate.
laibin-water-environment-displacement.displaced_label: families physically displaced, from the World Bank completion report's social safeguards section
laibin-water-environment-displacement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 2,014 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own count of people physically displaced is 2,363, in 416 families. Its total of affected people from all causes is 3,521, against 1,316 in the resettlement action plan.
laibin-water-environment-displacement.outcome: The loan closed on 31 January 2020 after a one-year extension, with US$14 million cancelled and misprocurement declared on one contract. The completion report records the resettlement as complete and satisfactorily implemented, with compensation paid on time and replacement apartments provided, and no grievances outstanding.

laibin-water-environment-displacement.conditions: The completion report records the project as triggering the involuntary resettlement policy because of the scale of land acquisition and involuntary resettlement, and cites it as OP/BP 4.11, which is the Bank's number for physical cultural resources rather than for resettlement. An environmental and social impact assessment and public consultation were carried out at preparation and again for the September 2017 restructuring, and a resettlement action plan was designed and implemented. Both volumes of the environmental management plan were disclosed in Laibin on 13 October 2012 and at the Bank's InfoShop on 11 December 2012, and the resettlement action plan was disclosed in Laibin on 30 October 2012 and at the InfoShop on 11 December 2012; both were updated at the 2017 restructuring and published locally on 27 December 2016 and on the Bank's website on 8 June 2017. The environmental assessment was category B on the ground that none of the four components caused serious environmental impacts. Independent consultants prepared and submitted annual external monitoring reports on the resettlement plan. The project management office set up a multilevel grievance redress mechanism with experienced staff to receive and address complaints (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 22 June 2020).

corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.title: Corumana Dam Resettlement Left Unfinished at Closing
corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.place: Corumana dam and the resettlement villages of Ndindiza, Fungotine, Baptine and Mutxipe, Moamba district, Maputo province, Mozambique
corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.point: The Corumana dam, Moamba district, Maputo province, whose completion the project financed and around which the resettlement took place (OpenStreetMap point for Barragem de Corumana)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-50110 of US$70 million and IDA-53070 of US$32 million for the National Water Resources Development Project (P107350), approved 15 September 2011. The revised commitment was US$96,958,920 and US$86,914,726 was disbursed. Original closing was 15 December 2017 and actual closing 30 June 2020, after a cumulative extension of 30.5 months that took the implementation period from six to 8.5 years. US$5 million was cancelled and reallocated to another Bank project for the response to Cyclones Idai and Kenneth in 2019. Environmental category A, full assessment. The implementing agency was the National Directorate of Water, later the National Directorate for Water Resources Management. The project budget for environmental and social compliance was US$6.5 million; the resettlement houses, access roads and boreholes alone came to nearly US$10 million, the electricity and water systems and the school and health centre works to a further US$7.6 million, and the consultancies, transport of affected people, auditors and preparation of agricultural land to US$5.9 million, with the gap covered by reallocating money from water resources development activities and from contingencies. The completion report of 20 May 2021 rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory on a split rating and put the risk to development outcome at Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review reached Moderately Satisfactory on outcome and Moderately Satisfactory on Bank performance (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 May 2021; IEG ICR Review ICRR0022601, Bank document date 3 November 2021).

companies.name: National Directorate for Water Resources Management (DNGRH)
companies.role: The directorate of the Mozambican Ministry of Public Works, Housing and Water Resources responsible for water resources management; it implemented the project and, with the regional water administration ARA-Sul, ran the grievance mechanism in the dam area and the resettlement villages. The completion report records its officials spending considerable time mediating with labour and the community, and intervening in contract management by registering threats of sanctions (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 May 2021).

corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.community: The project completed the Corumana dam on the Sabie river to raise the water available to greater Maputo. It financed 133 new houses at four sites with access roads, a water supply system, electricity and rehabilitation of the local school and health centre, serving both the people moved and the host communities. The completion report states that 660 project-affected people were resettled, and that each household was compensated with about two hectares of land prepared for farming plus cash for fruit trees and moving allowances. Updating the environmental and social impact assessment and the resettlement action plan took about four years and the Mozambican government approved them in April 2018, seven and a half years after the project became effective; the Bank took a further six months to approve the plan. Safeguards performance was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory again and again during those four years. Once the plan was approved, land acquisition and the financing of the houses moved quickly, but the parts of the plan the government was responsible for did not, for lack of capacity and budget. The dedicated consultant and service provider needed to carry out the resettlement were recruited only in December 2019 and February 2020, five months and three months before the project was due to close. In the meantime many of the newly built houses stood empty and were vandalised, with doors, locks and window fixtures stolen, so that on-site security was needed. The Bank's supervision missions in March and June 2018 called for caution in starting civil works because most of the households still to be resettled were living in the works area. The project closed on 30 June 2020 with parts of the resettlement plan and the livelihood restoration plan unfinished: auxiliary structures such as outside kitchens and barns, some compensation for commercial stalls, garages and warehouses, the relocation of existing gravesites, the issue of land and property titles, agricultural extension services, and the social and environmental audits. The government was responsible for land acquisition and for paying cash allowances and compensation, but by the time the plan began to be implemented the country had entered a fiscal crisis that severely limited the funds. The option of having the project itself pay the cash compensation was considered in 2017 and not pursued. Resettlement kits of farming and household tools were sourced from other government agencies and distributed, as were maize and bean seed. One worker was killed during construction in a vehicle accident the report calls preventable, whose root cause it puts mainly on the lack of senior management commitment in the contractor's organisation and to some extent on the borrower's inadequate capacity to manage safeguards. Occupational health and safety performance was poor at first and was corrected later through penalties, training and monitoring. Work stopped altogether on several occasions, including a five-week suspension in 2019 for non-compliance with health and safety requirements, intermittent labour stoppages and tensions in the local community, and a two-month hold on the saddle dam while unexploded ordnance found in the area was cleared.
corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.displaced_label: project-affected people resettled, from the World Bank completion report
corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 935 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's own count of people resettled is 660, into 133 houses at four sites. Delays in the census and socio-economic surveys made the number of affected people hard to settle, because each update recorded new families settling in the dam surroundings.
corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2020 with the resettlement plan and the livelihood restoration plan both unfinished and with some compensation and allowances unpaid. The Mozambican government was to finish and pay for the outstanding work with support from the panel of experts and the Bank, and the ministry later mobilised internal budget resources for it. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that it was not clear how committed the government was to financing and completing the pending activities. A grievance mechanism remained active in the dam area and in the four resettlement villages.

corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.confidence_note: The resettlement count, the unfinished compensation, the vandalised houses and the worker's death all come from the Bank's own completion report, and the unfinished compensation is confirmed by the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the Corumana resettlement was found. Two of the completion report's statements of fact are footnoted to personal communications with named Bank staff rather than to documents, and nothing here rests on those: the vandalism of the houses is footnoted to a personal communication of 4 February 2021, and the decision not to have the project fund cash compensation to one of 12 February 2021. The 660 resettled people, the 133 houses, the list of pending activities and the fatality are all in the report's own text. No document found names an affected household, says how many households the 660 people made up, or quantifies what compensation was still unpaid at closing. The review's safeguards section quotes the completion report's paragraph on occupational health and safety but omits the sentence about the fatality that follows it. The review carries no date anywhere on the page; the date used here is the Bank's own document date from its archive, unverified at document level.
corumana-dam-resettlement-mozambique.conditions: The project was environmental category A, full assessment, and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, safety of dams, involuntary resettlement and projects on international waterways. An environmental and social impact assessment, a social impact assessment, an environmental management plan and a resettlement action plan were prepared for the completion of the dam and disclosed in country and through the Bank's InfoShop. An environmental and social service provider was hired to review and update the assessment and the plan, both originally completed in 2011, to take account of new and more demanding Mozambican regulations on resettlement and economic impact assessment; that work took four years. The project design included a standalone component for safeguards compliance. Under the international waterways policy the government formally notified South Africa and Swaziland during preparation under the revised SADC protocol and the interim IncoMaputo agreement, and complied with South Africa's request for constant feedback through the Tripartite Permanent Technical Committee. Under the natural habitats policy, environmental flow requirements and water quality monitoring were built into the dam's operating management system, with base flow and freshet releases and a requirement to hold the dam below 117 metres above sea level except in severe floods, to limit backwater effects in the Sabie Game Reserve and Kruger National Park in South Africa. An emergency preparedness plan was prepared under the dam safety policy. The borrower was recommended to commission an independent environmental audit after the fatality; that audit found the contractor's environmental management partially compliant (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 20 May 2021; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 3 November 2021).

ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.title: Three Line Workers Killed and Compensation Paid Late on the Ethiopia-Sudan Interconnector
ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.place: The Bahir Dar to Gondar, Gondar to Shehedi and Shehedi to Metema transmission line, Amhara region, Ethiopia, to the Sudanese border at Gallabat
ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.point: Bahir Dar, the southern end of the line and the start of the Bahir Dar to Gondar section where construction began before the affected people had been paid (OpenStreetMap city point for Bahir Dar)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-43750 of SDR 26.44 million for the Ethiopia-Sudan Interconnector under the Nile Basin Initiative (P074011), approved 20 December 2007 and effective 31 July 2008, with SDR 24.37 million disbursed. Original closing was 31 December 2011 and actual closing 30 June 2013, after restructurings on 16 December 2011 and 14 June 2012. Environmental category B. The whole of the Bank's financing was coded to transmission and distribution of electricity. The implementing agencies were the Ministry of Water and Energy and the Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation. The completion report of 23 December 2013 rated outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Satisfactory and risk to development outcome Low; the Independent Evaluation Group's review posted 29 July 2014 agreed on outcome and gave risk to development outcome as Negligible to Low. Financial management was rated Moderately Unsatisfactory for most of implementation (Implementation Completion and Results Report ICR2925, 23 December 2013; IEG ICR Review, posted 29 July 2014).

companies.name: Energoinvest
companies.role: The subcontractor for the transmission line. It prepared the environmental, health and safety plan for the line works. The completion report records that over the course of construction three deaths and 11 accidents occurred, that the subcontractor neglected to require its personnel to use safety equipment such as safety belts and helmets, which contributed to the injuries, and that the inappropriate erection of two towers contributed to two tower collapses in 2010 that caused nine of the 11 accidents. The report records that the transmission line contractor paid compensation to the affected families and that the Bank team confirmed the payments were completed (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 December 2013).

companies.name: Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation (EEPCo)
companies.role: The Ethiopian state electricity utility, which was the project's implementing agency. It discussed safety practices with the subcontractor after the deaths and asked it to follow compensation procedures; it also paid ETB 25.11 million in compensation to project-affected people, and allowed the supervision engineer's contract to expire before the works were finished, so that supervision by environmental and social experts ended earlier than planned (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 December 2013).

ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.community: Despite the project's name, which carries the Nile Basin Initiative, the works were a high-voltage power link: 296.5 km of transmission line and the upgrading of three substations, running from Bahir Dar through Gondar and Shehedi to Metema on the Sudanese border, opposite Gallabat. The line involved expanding the existing 260 km single-circuit 230 kV line from Bahir Dar to Shehedi by building a second single-circuit system from Bahir Dar to Gondar and a second line on the existing double-circuit towers between Gondar and Shehedi, plus a new 36.5 km double-circuit 230/220 kV line from Shehedi to Metema. Three deaths and 11 accidents occurred during construction of the line. One worker was killed in June 2010 through negligence, having used no scaffolding or care when crossing a road to string a line. Two more were killed in 2011 in an accident during the erection of a tower, having not worn safety belts. Nine of the 11 accidents came from two tower collapses in 2010 caused by towers being put up wrongly. The completion report states that the Bank team requested and received information on the compensation paid to the families of the dead. On the resettlement side, construction work started on the Bahir Dar to Gondar section before the affected people had received their compensation; the utility had to be told so that the construction schedule could be changed to pay first, and three of the woredas, the district administrations, delayed their payments, which held up completion of that line by eight months. Of the 4,490 affected people, five families were paid compensation for damage to their property but received no land, because they held no legal ownership title from the local government and Ethiopian law makes title a condition of land compensation. Three of those five families refused to move and went to court for redress. They lost their appeals. The Bank recommended that the utility arrange special assistance for their relocation anyway, the utility asked the districts to consider it, and the completion report states that the families have been successfully relocated since the project closed. In total ETB 25.11 million, about US$1.39 million, was paid in compensation to 4,490 affected people.
ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,415 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's own completion report counts 4,490 affected people paid compensation. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated, except the five families denied land compensation, of whom three refused to move and were relocated after the project closed.
ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.suppression: Three of the five families who were paid for damage to their property but given no land refused to move and sought redress in the courts. They lost their appeals, and the completion report states they were relocated after the project closed.
ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.outcome: The credit closed on 30 June 2013 after an 18-month extension, with the line sections completed in August 2010 and 2011 and the substations late. The completion report records the environmental management plan and the resettlement action plan as implemented by closing. The three families who had refused to move were relocated after the project closed, with special assistance the Bank recommended after they had lost in court.

ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.confidence_note: The deaths, the accidents, their causes, the construction that began before compensation was paid and the five families denied land compensation all come from the Bank's own completion report; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report repeats the same account of the deaths almost word for word. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of these deaths or of this line's land acquisition was found. Both documents record the compensation as late. The completion report says work began on the Bahir Dar to Gondar section before the affected people were paid and that three woredas delayed payments, costing eight months; the review's section on administrative efficiency says outstanding compensation owed by the district administrations caused delays and rescheduling of work, with an overall delay of eight months, and its section on government performance lists ensuring that compensation payments were timely among the things a higher level of government input could have achieved. The documents give no names, no dates for the five families' court cases, no date for their relocation and no figure for what the three woredas owed. The three deaths are counted here because the report names their causes: negligence in crossing a road to string a line, and personnel not wearing safety belts during a tower erection, after a subcontractor that did not require safety equipment to be used. The report does not say whether the dead were employees of the subcontractor or of anyone else. The amount paid to the families of the dead is not given in any document found.
ethiopia-sudan-interconnector-line-death.conditions: The project was environmental category B and triggered the policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. An environmental and social impact assessment containing an environmental management plan, with resettlement action plans for Ethiopia and for Sudan, was prepared with support from the Eastern Nile Technical Regional Office of the Nile Basin Initiative, and the Bank disclosed the management plan and the two plans in the two countries in 2007. Monitoring of safeguards was to be done by the supervision engineer, with auditing and implementation by the Ethiopian Electric Power Corporation and independent monitoring and oversight by the regional office, which also served as the Bank team's route for information on the Sudanese portion. Implementation of both plans was completed by closing, with adjustments to synchronise the resettlement plan with the revised construction timetable. The utility let the supervision engineer's contract expire before the facilities were finished rather than extend it as the Bank team suggested, so supervision by environmental and social experts ended earlier than planned, and a restructuring of the utility's environment management unit during implementation further weakened its monitoring. Ethiopian law makes a legal ownership title issued by the local government a condition of land compensation, which is why five families who lost property received cash but no land (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 December 2013).

gameleira-agrovila-ceara.title: Two Years Without Water or Power in the Gameleira Resettlement Village, Ceara
gameleira-agrovila-ceara.place: Gameleira dam agrovila, on the rural boundary of Itapipoca, Trairi and Tururu, Ceara, Brazil, and the Umari and Jenipapeiro dam resettlements at Madalena and Baixio
gameleira-agrovila-ceara.point: Itapipoca, the municipality the Bank's completion report gives for the Gameleira dam; Agencia Publica places the dam on the boundary of the rural areas of Trairi, Itapipoca and Tururu, about 150 km from Fortaleza (OpenStreetMap administrative point for Itapipoca)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-76300 of US$103.0 million, the additional financing to the Ceara Integrated Water Resources Management Project, PROGERIRH (P110487), for the same objectives as the original loan IBRD-45310 for P006449. The completion report's data sheet gives approval on 18 December 2008 and its text says the Board approved it on 17 December 2008; it was signed only in September 2009 and became effective in November 2009, with a closing date of December 2011, leaving an effective two-year implementation period. US$98.33 million of the additional loan was disbursed. Delays in signing came from the procedures for processing loans between the federal government and the state and the need for Senate approval. Across both phases the original commitment was US$136 million and US$237.28 million was disbursed. Environmental category A. The implementing agency was the state Secretariat of Water Resources, with the water company COGERH and the works superintendence SOHIDRA executing parts of it. The completion report of 28 December 2012 rated outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and downgraded overall safeguard compliance to Moderately Unsatisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review posted 21 June 2013 agreed on outcome, put risk to development outcome at High against the report's Moderate, and rated Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory against the report's Moderately Satisfactory (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012; IEG ICR Review, posted 21 June 2013).

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD), first phase
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-45310 for the original Ceara Integrated Water Resources Management Project (P006449), approved 6 January 2000 and effective 24 May 2000, which built the first six dams. The additional financing built five more (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012).

companies.name: EIT
companies.role: The contractor on the Gameleira dam and agrovila works, named by Agencia Publica, which reports that the firm entered judicial recovery during construction and could not complete the works, that the state secretariat suspended payments to it in August 2011 by court order and that the works stopped in December 2011, by which time families had been living in the agrovila since January of that year. A state audit prosecutor's representation of March 2012 was filed against the secretariat and against EIT (Agencia Publica, 16 April 2015).

companies.name: Secretaria dos Recursos Hidricos do Ceara (SRH)
companies.role: The water resources secretariat of the state government of Ceara, the project's main implementing agency. It maintained special units to manage resettlement and the environment and to coordinate environmental mitigation and compensation. The completion report rates its performance under the additional financing Moderately Unsatisfactory, citing insufficient action on construction delays and inadequate attention to resettlement and environmental mitigation works, and says its supervision capacity was not strong enough in the later years (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012).

companies.name: Superintendencia de Obras Hidraulicas (SOHIDRA)
companies.role: The state works superintendence of Ceara, responsible for surveillance of contractors' performance. The state government decided to stop using an external supervision firm, against an agreement with the Bank that external supervision would run throughout implementation, and to supervise through SOHIDRA instead; the completion report states that SOHIDRA was not adequately staffed or trained to supervise environmental and social aspects of the contractors' work, and that this affected the quality of supervision of the works and the environmental mitigation activities (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012).

gameleira-agrovila-ceara.community: Across the two phases the project built 11 dams and affected 2,174 families: 1,394 under the first phase's six dams and 780 under the additional financing's five, at Gameleira in Itapipoca, Umari in Madalena, Jatoba in Ipueiras, Jenipapeiro in Baixio and Mamoeiro in Antonina do Norte. The completion report's resettlement table sets out what each family received. Of the 2,174, 261 families took houses in new agricultural villages, the agrovilas, with infrastructure and a farm plot; 377 were resettled on unaffected parts of their own farms; 491 bought new homes themselves with a resettlement grant; and 12 bought homes in nearby towns, making 1,141 families moved. The remaining 1,033 were landowners who took cash compensation, for whom the report records no move. Under the additional financing alone 140 families went into agrovilas and 185 to remaining areas, 87 resettled themselves and 368 took cash. The families resettled into the Gameleira agrovila in January 2011 had no water or electricity supply until December 2012, nearly two years, despite repeated recommendations and alerts from the Bank's supervision missions in 2011 and 2012. By December 2012 the handover of their farm plots was still unfinished because the demarcation was incomplete, and neither the land titles nor the fencing of the agrovila had been resolved. The completion report states that the titling of lots had not been done in any of the agrovilas the project financed under either phase. At Jenipapeiro the dam was filled in 2011 before the power line running through the reservoir basin had been moved, which left the families settled in the agrovila without power and therefore without water, because their supply depended on electric pumps; the problem was solved in early 2012 after intense effort by Bank missions. At Umari the 35 houses the project built in 2011 developed structural problems and had to be demolished and rebuilt, which the original contractor did at no extra cost in groups of five houses while the families were moved temporarily into houses rented by the government; the completion report says this poor construction quality should have been identified during the works and was being resolved only in December 2012, more than a year after they were finished. Fourteen compensation cases were still open at December 2012, all of them landowners who had taken cash and were still disputing the valuation of their land; most had had 80 per cent of the amount deposited as a court bond. Agencia Publica reported on the Gameleira agrovila in April 2015. It gives the dam's cost as R$40 million, R$18 million of it World Bank money, and 180 families affected according to the state secretariat, 91 of them living on the site and losing part or all of their land. It records that EIT entered judicial recovery during construction of the agrovila and could not finish the works. It reports one resident receiving R$7,000 in indemnity and another saying each house was paid R$5,000, against a secretariat ceiling of R$12,000 for owners who lost more than two-thirds of their land. It found the agrovila's only water source to be a well with a desalination unit treating about a quarter of the water used each day, giving each family 36 litres a day for drinking and cooking and leaving the salty well water for everything else; the pipeline that was the original plan, for a minimum capacity of 30,000 litres, had never been built, and although a contract of about R$250,000 had been awarded to another firm, I. C. Projetos e Construcoes, the work had not started. Power arrived only in late 2012, after the electricity company Coelce cut an illegal connection in January 2012. The health post was an empty concrete shell and the refuse collection and leisure areas were never delivered. The association president Paulo Sergio de Moraes Alves told the reporters that people there had to go on using the salty water, and that a water tanker could take days to arrive. A resident, Maria Socorro, said they had not been compensated but humoured into leaving. In March 2012 a state prosecutor at the state audit court filed a representation describing the families' conditions as sub-human. The Bank told the reporters that its missions had found the water supply adequate. The same report gives figures for the first phase's Aracoiaba dam, finished in December 2002 at about R$14 million, which affected 608 families, 333 of them living on the site, and also faced low compensation and incomplete agrovilas, and says that World Bank-financed works in Ceara affected at least 4,625 families according to the state secretariat.
gameleira-agrovila-ceara.displaced_label: families moved under the four resettlement options in the World Bank completion report's resettlement table (261 into agrovilas, 377 onto remaining parts of their own farms, 491 self-resettled, 12 into towns); 412 of them under this additional financing
gameleira-agrovila-ceara.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,176 for this additional financing, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's resettlement table counts families, not people: 780 families affected under the additional financing's five dams and 1,394 under the first phase's six, 2,174 in all. Of those 2,174, the table's own columns give 261 resettled into agrovilas, 377 onto unaffected parts of their own farms, 491 self-resettled with a grant and 12 into homes in towns, which is 1,141 families moved; the other 1,033 were landowners who took cash compensation and whose movement the report does not record. Under the additional financing alone the four relocation options come to 412 families of 780. Agencia Publica gives 180 families affected at Gameleira on the state secretariat's figures, 91 of them living on the site, which matches the completion report's total of 180 for that dam.
gameleira-agrovila-ceara.outcome: The additional financing closed in December 2012 with two of its five dams complete and three still under construction, at 75 per cent for Gameleira, 92 per cent for Mamoeiro and 96 per cent for Jatoba, and with all six of its planned conveyance pipelines unfinished. The Ipaumirim pipeline works were halted by a judicial dispute between the contractor and the implementing agency. The Bank said it would keep supervising the pending works and resettlement activities into 2013. Overall safeguard compliance was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review found the state had departed from the procedures agreed with the Bank and so was not in compliance with the resettlement policy, particularly on the timely payment of fair compensation to those displaced, with long delays in issuing land titles for agrovila residents. The review records that many resettlement issues, especially titling and compensation, remained outstanding. By April 2015 Agencia Publica found the Gameleira agrovila still without the pipeline that had been planned and still drinking desalinated well water.

gameleira-agrovila-ceara.confidence_note: The resettlement counts, the dates, the two years without water or power at Gameleira, the rebuilt houses at Umari, the Jenipapeiro power line and the missing land titles come from the Bank's own completion report, and the finding of non-compliance with the resettlement policy and the outstanding titling and compensation come from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The compensation amounts residents received, the state audit prosecutor's representation of March 2012, the unbuilt pipeline, the daily 36 litres and the resident accounts come from Agencia Publica's field report of 16 April 2015, which is the independent source here and names the people it quotes. That report and the Bank documents are consistent on the figure of 180 families at Gameleira and on the resettlement date of January 2011 and the arrival of water and power in December 2012. The completion report gives the additional financing's approval date twice and differently, as 18 December 2008 in its data sheet and 17 December 2008 in its text. The contractor EIT is named only by Agencia Publica, which does not give its full legal name, and the Bank documents name no contractor. The firm awarded the unbuilt pipeline contract, I. C. Projetos e Construcoes, is a different company. No document found says how many people the 2,174 families comprised, or how many of the 14 open compensation cases were later settled.
gameleira-agrovila-ceara.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, natural habitats, pest management, physical cultural resources, involuntary resettlement and dam safety. A regional environmental assessment covering five river basins was carried out during preparation of the original project, and environmental assessments and management plans for the large hydraulic works were approved by the Bank before appraisal in 1999 and before approval of the additional financing in 2008. Bank review and approval were required for any proposed reservoir, each of which needed an acceptable resettlement plan and an environmental impact assessment and management plan. Works contracts had to oblige the contractor to clear vegetation in the inundation area and to mark or fence the permanent protection strip on the reservoir margin, and an environmental construction manual was produced to guide supervision. Supervision of the works by private consultant firms was to cover the contractors' compliance with the safeguards and the management plans; the state government discontinued that external supervision during the additional financing, against its agreement with the Bank. Every family was to be offered a choice between resettling itself with a grant and being resettled in an agrovila with a farm plot. Brazil has no resettlement law, and the completion report calls the secretariat's effort to carry out resettlement to Bank rules within the Brazilian legal framework commendable. Dam interventions were evaluated by a safety panel set up for the purpose (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 December 2012; IEG ICR Review, posted 21 June 2013).

patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.title: Riverbank Dwellers Moved Late and Three Workers Killed on the Ganga Clean-up
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.place: The Patna riverfront development on the Ganga, including Bhairwa Ghat and the Digha sewage treatment plant site, and the Beur and Begusarai works, Bihar, India
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.point: Patna, where the riverfront development was the only project investment requiring full land acquisition, affecting 249 families, and where the Digha and Beur sites lie (OpenStreetMap city point for Patna)

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA and IBRD)
lenders.role: Credit IDA-49550 of US$199 million and loan IBRD-80650 of US$801 million for the National Ganga River Basin Project (P119085), approved 31 May 2011 and effective 18 August 2011. The IBRD loan was cut to US$334,825,259 and US$514,233,533 was disbursed in all against the original US$1 billion commitment. Original closing was 31 December 2019 and actual closing 30 December 2021. Total project cost fell from US$1.556 billion to US$673,583,533. Environmental category A, full assessment. The implementing agency was the National Mission for Clean Ganga in the Ministry of Jal Shakti. The project financing agreement was revised to include the provisions of India's Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013. Safeguards performance at closing was rated Moderately Satisfactory. The completion report of 28 February 2023 rated outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation quality Substantial; the Independent Evaluation Group's review agreed on all three (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 29 June 2023).

companies.name: National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG)
companies.role: The mission under the Department of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation in India's Ministry of Jal Shakti that implemented the project, working through state programme management groups. The completion report records that the programme management groups had dedicated systems for safeguards implementation, and that procurement capacity at state level and at the Central Pollution Control Board remained low (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023).

patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.community: The project financed sewage treatment plants, sewer networks and a riverfront development to cut pollution going into the Ganga. Most investments used land already under existing treatment plants or government land transferred after a no-objection certificate, and where private land was needed the project bought it directly; the completion report records that direct purchase was dogged by prolonged price negotiations, contested ownership rights and complications in paying the final amounts. The only investment that required full land acquisition was the Patna riverfront development, which affected 249 families. Those affected were encroachers living in shacks and mud houses on the riverbank. Because compensation against the existing value of their assets and income would have been negligible, a flat rate of INR 150,000 and land for a house were agreed instead. The land allotment was then stalled for two years, and in the end extra cash was given instead of land. The completion report records a further complication: the sites were handed over to the contractor before the affected people had been resettled and before compensation was paid. The affected people were tracked down and compensated, and the report says this affected implementation of the investment, especially at Bhairwa Ghat. Beyond the riverfront, 20 households were affected by partial land acquisition and 234 households by economic losses. At closing all resettlement action plans had been fully implemented and one abbreviated plan was still open, to compensate three affected people at the Digha sewage treatment plant site. All the riverfront families were eventually compensated and given training to restore their incomes. In 2021 two fatal incidents at project sites in Bihar killed three labourers, one at Begusarai in March and two at Beur in May. The completion report's annex on the project's history states that the root-cause analysis indicated the accidents occurred through negligence on occupational health and safety training of workers and supervisors; its safeguards section says the root-cause analysis of both incidents pointed at gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice, and the Bank's own supervision records had reported unsatisfactory performance on those points across the whole implementation period of the works component. After the deaths the incident reporting procedures were followed, the next of kin were compensated, a safety audit was carried out and regular on-site briefings were held. The completion report states that three workers died under circumstances that appear to have been preventable, and that site management and worker safety remained a perennial concern from the start of the works component, with the outcome proving unsatisfactory in Begusarai and Beur. On procurement, Bank guidelines were violated and misprocurement was declared on the Buxar sewage treatment plant and sewerage works, confidential information was leaked during the bid evaluation for the Munger sewage treatment plant and sewerage network, and preliminary bid evaluation reports prepared by implementing agencies were contested by the mission and the Bank and had to be revised. All three instances were in Bihar.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.displaced_label: project-affected families on the Patna riverfront, from the World Bank completion report; the report calls them project affected families and does not separately count those physically moved
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,103 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 249 project-affected families at the Patna riverfront development, the only investment requiring full land acquisition, plus 20 households affected by partial land acquisition and 234 households affected by economic losses, and three people still to be compensated at the Digha site at closing.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.outcome: The project closed on 30 December 2021 after a two-year extension, with US$466 million of the original US$1 billion commitment never used. All resettlement plans were recorded as implemented except one abbreviated plan covering three people at the Digha site. The Digha-Kankerbagh contract was carried forward to the Second National Ganga River Basin Project. The riverfront families received cash instead of the land they had been promised. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the completion report's account of the three deaths and of the one outstanding plan, but does not mention the 249 families, the two-year delay in the land allotment, or the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled and paid; its summary says that all project-affected families were eventually compensated.

patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.confidence_note: The 249 families, the two-year stall in the land allotment, the handing of sites to the contractor before people were resettled and paid, and the three deaths all come from the Bank's own completion report; the review of that report by the Independent Evaluation Group repeats the deaths and the single outstanding plan but not the rest. The lender is reporting on its own project and no independent account of the Patna riverfront resettlement or of the two fatal incidents was found; a web search returned Indian press reports on other Ganga riverbank evictions and bridge projects in Bihar, none of them tied to this project. The three deaths are counted here because the report names a cause: its safeguards section gives gaps in site management and occupational health and safety practice and calls the circumstances apparently preventable, and its project-history annex gives negligence on occupational health and safety training of workers and supervisors. The same annex places one death at Begusarai in March 2021 and two at Beur in May 2021. The documents do not say who employed the dead. They name no affected family, do not say how many people the 249 families comprised, and do not say how much extra cash was paid in place of the promised land. The report also records that all the affected families were eventually compensated and trained for income restoration. The review carries no date anywhere on the page; the date used here is the Bank's own document date from its archive, unverified at document level.
patna-ganga-riverfront-resettlement.conditions: The project was environmental category A and triggered the policies on environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, physical cultural resources, natural habitats and projects on international waterways. A resettlement policy and land acquisition framework was included in the environmental and social management framework and used throughout. Environmental management plans, social management plans and resettlement action plans for high-impact investments were prepared by third parties. The investment framework required priority to be given to land already under existing treatment plants or to government land transferred with a no-objection certificate, then to direct purchase, and only to compulsory acquisition where unavoidable; where it was used, resettlement plans and abbreviated plans were prepared and disclosed. The financing agreement was revised during implementation to include the provisions of India's Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act 2013. The indigenous peoples policy was triggered by the presence of scheduled tribes, with the largest population in Jharkhand, where a dedicated consultation was held and a tribal management framework prepared; only Sahibganj district had a substantial tribal population and the investment there affected no tribal settlement. Under the international waterways policy China, Nepal and Bangladesh were notified and raised no objection. The physical cultural resources policy was triggered by possible effects of the riverfront development on cultural properties on the banks of the Ganga; the Patna environmental assessment identified religious sites that could be affected and the design was made to avoid them, so no management plan was required. A strategic environmental and social assessment was completed in March 2020 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 28 February 2023).

lenders.role: Credits IDA-51050 of US$500 million, IDA-62770 of US$300 million and IDA-62780 of US$100 million for the Nigeria Erosion and Watershed Management Project (P124905), approved 8 May 2012 and effective 16 September 2013, with additional financing approved 27 June 2018 (P164082). companies.name: Federal Ministry of Environment, National Project Implementation Unit
companies.role: The unit within Nigeria's federal environment ministry that ran the project nationally, with state project management units in each participating state. The completion report records that the unit's database of the status of every resettlement action plan by state was used to monitor each state's progress, and that the project developed social safeguards guidelines for the ministry (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 July 2023).

newmap-nigeria-erosion-displacement.community: The project treated gully erosion and watershed sites, beginning in seven states, Anambra, Abia, Cross River, Ebonyi, Edo, Enugu and Imo, and scaling up to 23. It supported communities inside treated sites either by compensating them for lost productive assets and activities, through 83 resettlement action plans that the completion report says benefited 9,471 affected people, or through livelihood activities. By 31 October 2022 the project had compensated 9,696 affected people and fully implemented 94 resettlement action plans over its ten years. At closing 21 of the 23 states had fully implemented their plans. Two states, Abia and Imo, could not locate 32 affected people, and an escrow account was opened and funded with counterpart money to pay them if they came forward. Imo State was still implementing its resettlement plan at closing, with the compensation money held in an escrow account. Unfinished civil works remained in three states, which the completion report says could lead to the destruction of properties, the displacement of people or public risk; every affected state except Imo prepared and carried out an exit plan with measures including cordoning off the unfinished sites with signs, telling the people who would have benefited about the risk, and securing a binding commitment from the state to finish the works. Imo State provided no letter of comfort for its unfinished sites. Over the project's life more than 1,160 complaints were received across the 23 states and all were recorded as resolved. Three workers died at project sites. The report records the deaths as occupational health and safety fatalities, each of which triggered the Bank's environmental and social incident response procedure, and says the root-cause analyses found them not systemic but one-off cases; it gives no cause for any of the three. The report's economic analysis, in valuing the displacement the works avoided, uses a figure of 5,721 project-affected people actually displaced by the project, drawn from resettlement plan implementation reports at 84 sites, and then extrapolates to 7,015 while referring to 81 sites. Sub-grants for livelihood activities such as waste management, livestock farming, plant nurseries, gabion box welding and block moulding reached 35,977 beneficiaries by closing, of whom the report gives 15,977 as male and 20,509 as female, figures that come to 36,486 rather than 35,977.
newmap-nigeria-erosion-displacement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,087 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated in the project's safeguards reporting. The figure of 5,721 "project-affected persons (PAPs) actually displaced by the project" appears once, in the completion report's economic analysis, as the input to Benefit 4 of the benefit-cost calculation at closing, "Avoided involuntary displacement of people": the passage divides resettlement spending by that number to derive an average of US$3,453 a person and so value the displacement the works avoided. The same bullet then extrapolates to 7,015 people while switching from 84 project sites to 81, without explaining either the new total or the change in sites, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review, which rates the quality of the completion report Modest, does not carry 5,721 or 7,015 at all. A number used as an input to a benefit calculation is not the document's count of people displaced, so it is not entered here. The counts the report gives in its social safeguards section are 9,696 affected people compensated as of 31 October 2022 under 94 resettlement action plans fully implemented, and 9,471 affected people benefiting from 83 plans.
newmap-nigeria-erosion-displacement.killed_note: Three workers died at project sites. The World Bank's completion report of 19 July 2023 records them in its environmental safeguards section as occupational health and safety fatalities that triggered the Bank's environmental and social incident response procedure, and says the root-cause analyses found they were not systemic issues but one-off cases. The report gives no cause, no date, no place and no identity for any of the three, and the Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the same account without adding any. They are therefore not counted.
newmap-nigeria-erosion-displacement.outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2022 after a two-year extension. Twenty-one of 23 states had fully implemented their resettlement plans; Imo State had not, and its compensation money was left in an escrow account, as was the money for the 32 people Abia and Imo could not find. Civil works were unfinished in three states, with the state governments committed to completing them as part of the borrower's responsibility. The completion report's own recommendation was to focus counterpart funding on compensating affected people in each state.

Two environmental and social audits were carried out by third-party consultants, both with satisfactory findings. Each state financed the whole of its compensation from counterpart funds, and the completion report attributes part of the project's efficiency to the states allocating those funds on time. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that the completion report gives no specific information on action taken under the natural habitats, pest management, physical cultural resources, international waterways and dam safety policies (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 19 July 2023; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 10 November 2023).
