companies.name: Department of Local Infrastructure Development and Agricultural Roads (DOLIDAR)
companies.role: The department of Nepal's local development ministry responsible for rural infrastructure and agricultural roads, which implemented the project through its project coordination unit and district technical offices. Audits of the project reported large advance payments made in the last month of the fiscal year to avoid the budget being frozen, delays in settling advances given by District Development Committees, and misuse of the project's assets (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 June 2014; IEG ICR Review, posted 31 March 2015).

nepal-raidp-land-donation.community: The project upgraded and rehabilitated existing rural roads, tracks and trails in 20 districts and then 10 more. The roads were built largely on land the communities gave up. The completion report states that the community donated 2.13 million square metres of land, which at prevailing market rates it estimates at NPR 5.63 billion, about US$56.3 million, and that this is several times more than the NPR 64.4 million, about US$0.65 million, that the project provided as assistance to the affected people. The report presents this as a noteworthy feature of community involvement. It also records that implementation of the social safeguard requirements was so slow at first that at the mid-term review in November 2008 it was rated highly unsatisfactory, among other things because of non-payment of compensation to severely project affected families, there being no resettlement action plan as required. In response the project coordination unit assessed the impacts of the voluntary land donation and the numbers of affected families and prepared a remedial action plan, whose implementation resolved 97 per cent of the land ownership issues by the end of the project. The remaining owners could not be compensated: they were either absentee landowners or their land was in litigation. In total there were 12,558 affected families, of which 204 severely affected families, 162 for land, 37 for structures and 5 for loss of livelihood, had received their assistance by the end of the project. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, summarising page 8 of the report, states that the report also gives 11,460 of 11,866 landowners as compensated; at that point in the published completion report the figures sit inside a parenthesis that is blank in the document's text, so the review's summary is the only place the pair can be read. The report's borrower annex records that the project awarded a letter of appreciation to all 11,866 land donors and displayed their names in public places. Those who donated more than 10 per cent of their holding were compensated for the part above 10 per cent. Transfer of donated land titles was completed for 97.1 per cent under the additional financing, which the borrower's own report attributes to landowners being unavailable and to a few disputed cases. The Independent Evaluation Group's review calls the completion report's treatment of the resettlement policy confusing on four counts: it is unclear how far the Bank scrutinised the voluntary land donation process, which the review says can lead to abuse through forceful land acquisition; the report says there were 12,558 affected families of which only the 204 severely affected received compensation, then says 11,460 of 11,866 landowners were compensated, without stating whether those totals include the donors and the severely affected families; it is unknown how many people were actually compensated during implementation or whether the compensation was adequate; and the report is inconsistent in its rating of social safeguards, giving Satisfactory in one paragraph and Moderately Satisfactory in another. The review's own lesson is that voluntary donation of land transfers for project activities may lead to abuse, and that careful monitoring by the Bank can help ensure that abuse does not occur and that the donation is genuinely voluntary. The borrower's own section of the completion report says that all the roads upgraded under the additional financing were existing roads and caused minimum negative social impact, and that the project did not displace a single individual. Environmental safeguards were a concern until late 2012 because of delays in preparing the initial environmental examinations and management plans, in designing site-specific mitigation works and in carrying them out; performance varied from road to road between moderately unsatisfactory and moderately satisfactory.
nepal-raidp-land-donation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,028 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 12,558 affected families, 11,866 land donors and 204 severely affected families. The borrower's own section of the same report states that the project did not displace a single individual, and no Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
nepal-raidp-land-donation.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2013 after a three-year extension. Social safeguards ended with a rating the completion report gives twice and differently, as Satisfactory in one paragraph and Moderately Satisfactory in another, after a highly unsatisfactory rating at mid-term for non-payment of compensation. Ninety-seven per cent of land ownership issues were resolved; the rest were absentee owners or land in litigation. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that it is unknown how many people were actually compensated during implementation or whether the compensation was adequate.

nepal-raidp-land-donation.conditions: The project was environmental category B because the civil works were small in scale, upgrading existing dry-weather roads to all-weather roads, upgrading existing tracks and trails to dry-weather roads, and maintaining existing district roads. Besides environmental assessment it triggered the policies on cultural property, involuntary resettlement and indigenous peoples. The appraisal document records that the department prepared an environmental and social management framework setting out how social screening would assess the project's effect on households, how voluntary land donations would be recorded, and how the institutional structure for managing social impacts, including monitoring and evaluation, would be assessed. The appraisal document also notes that although no involuntary resettlement was expected, a resettlement policy framework was completed in case of minor land acquisition, and a vulnerable communities development framework was prepared so that indigenous, tribal, minority and vulnerable groups were not adversely affected. No resettlement action plan existed at the point when compensation went unpaid to severely affected families, and one was prepared only as part of the remedial action plan that followed the mid-term review. The framework provided for consultation with affected people and disclosure through the local road users' and village road coordination committees. Twenty social mobilisers and a social development expert were engaged. The framework was updated during preparation of the additional financing, after which environmental specialists were assigned to the project (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 24 June 2014; IEG ICR Review, posted 31 March 2015).

companies.name: Office National de l'Eau et de l'Assainissement (ONEA)
companies.role: Burkina Faso's national water and sanitation utility, a state-owned company, which implemented the project and whose environmental and social unit was responsible for the safeguard instruments. The Independent Evaluation Group's review records that it started the Ouagadougou water transmission civil works funded under the additional financing without preparing a resettlement action plan and without compensating four project-affected people, which brought the works to a halt. The completion report records that it expressed a preference for compensating affected people after the works rather than before (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 17 December 2020; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 24 June 2021).

ouagadougou-onea-works-before-compensati.community: The project extended water production, storage and distribution and sanitation in Ouagadougou, Bobo-Dioulasso and three other urban centres. Six original subprojects required compensation payments to landowners: secondary water distribution networks in Bobo-Dioulasso, Dedougou and Koudougou, boreholes in Bobo-Dioulasso and Dedougou, and a distribution line in Koudougou. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that no physical settlement occurred because of those six. Under the additional financing the utility began the Ouagadougou water transmission civil works without preparing a resettlement action plan and without compensating four project-affected people, which breaches the Bank's resettlement policy. The Bank was informed in December 2016 and the works were suspended on 15 December 2016. The Bank and the utility agreed an action plan to bring the project back into compliance, the utility prepared a resettlement plan, the Bank approved it in April 2017, and the suspension of the civil works was lifted in June 2017. The two documents count the people left unpaid at different moments and do not agree on how many there were in all. The review states that, excluding 49 project-affected people who could not be located, all the other 768 were compensated by May 2017, and that the compensation amounts for the 49 were deposited in an escrow account for future payment, which makes 817 people. The completion report, written at closing in December 2020, states that some affected people remained unfound despite three reminders from the project and could not be compensated, giving 26 of 756 affected people on lot 2.2 and 4 of 79 on lot 6.1, which is 30 of 835, and that the utility opened an escrow account holding their compensation in case they came forward. The number unpaid is therefore lower at closing than in May 2017, while the number of affected people is 18 higher, and neither document explains either figure or says which lots the review's 817 covers. The completion report also records that where works started late the utility faced complaints from people trying to settle on the land after it had been secured, and that its social and environmental specialists stressed the importance of keeping records so that evidence of compensation and of eligibility would not be missing.
ouagadougou-onea-works-before-compensati.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 1,953 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Independent Evaluation Group's review states that no physical settlement occurred because of the six original subprojects that required compensation, and counts 817 project-affected people on the additional financing's Ouagadougou works, of whom 768 were compensated by May 2017; the completion report's two lots on the same works come to 835 affected people, of whom 30 were never compensated. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
ouagadougou-onea-works-before-compensati.outcome: The project closed on 31 December 2019 with a Satisfactory safeguards rating. The suspension of the Ouagadougou civil works was lifted in June 2017 once a resettlement plan had been written and approved and the people who could be found had been paid. The compensation for those who could not be found, 49 people by the Independent Evaluation Group's count or 30 by the completion report's, was left in an escrow account to be paid if they came forward.

ouagadougou-onea-works-before-compensati.conditions: The project was environmental category B, because the construction works had minimal, site-specific and manageable environmental impacts, and triggered the policy on involuntary resettlement. Because the specific areas of intervention could not be confirmed before appraisal, the utility prepared an environmental and social management framework and a resettlement policy framework instead of project-specific instruments; both were disclosed to the public in Burkina Faso on 30 January 2009 and at the Bank's InfoShop on 6 February 2009, and both were updated and redisclosed in Burkina Faso and at the InfoShop on 5 June 2014 at the time of the additional financing. The management framework set out a screening mechanism for construction, waste disposal and the operation and maintenance of the water and sanitation works. Work-specific environmental and social impact assessments and resettlement action plans were prepared during implementation, approved by the National Bureau of Environmental Assessments and implemented; the project's fourth component paid for preparing the assessments. The utility's environmental and social unit was responsible for implementation. Municipalities took part in carrying out the resettlement plans and in resolving complaints through the grievance redress mechanism, and a resettlement committee was set up for each area and then reused for other projects. The completion report records the utility noting a lack of flexibility over the mismatch between the national practice of compensating and the Bank's requirement (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 17 December 2020; IEG ICR Review, Bank document date 24 June 2021).

fields_add.community: The World Bank's completion report of 26 June 2019 for the same project, P108143, records the outcome. The dam and its ancillary works were designed to keep physical displacement to a minimum, and only six households needed relocation under the Replacement Housing Program; their replacement houses were completed and used. Across the contract work areas there were 2,798 affected households, of whom 2,615 had received compensation by closing, 93 per cent of the target. Disbursement of compensation was still going on when the project closed on 31 December 2018, with 183 cases, 6.5 per cent, outstanding; M 59.36 million had been paid and M 3.82 million, 6 per cent, was still to be paid. The Metolong Authority judged that more than 107 of the outstanding cases could be completed without difficulty. The remaining 76 were 36 cases in dispute in the courts and 40 cases of people who had migrated to South Africa or elsewhere. The report attributes the outstanding disputes to arguments over who owned the affected property, to the compensation amounts, which in some cases led people not to claim the money due to them, and to the difficulty of finding people who had moved away. The main cause of the delay was compensation tied to rural electrification work, whose scope grew from 35 villages to 80 and which was carried out late in the programme. Of the affected households, 550 were headed by women and almost 10 per cent of household heads were disabled, so the compensation programme added specific measures for them. The report also records that errors were made in valuing assets, which led to compensation requirements being overestimated; the valuation methods were then adjusted, disputes arose, compensation was delayed, and the ombudsman had to be brought in to reach a settlement. In 2012 the dam contractor began construction and blasting without an approved environmental protection plan, a blasting plan, a blasting method statement, a mining permit, an approved evacuation plan or a satisfactory dilapidation survey; some activities were suspended, and complaints followed an uncontrolled blast in August 2012. There were ten fatalities during implementation of the Metolong programme, all of which the report says were properly reported and settled under Lesotho's Labour Code. A livelihood restoration programme trained the two affected communities of Ratau and Motanasela in poultry, pig-keeping, value chains, group dynamics, conflict resolution and social cohesion, and both communities set up trust funds managed by Standard Lesotho Bank. Implementation of the resettlement action plan was not finished when the project closed, and the Bank said it would keep supervising until the end of 2019. In March 2019 the government extended the Metolong Authority's mandate to October 2019 to finish the compensation payments and the livelihood work, and made a budget provision of M 1,800,000 for pending compensation. In February 2026 GroundUp reported that the communities around the dam still had no tap water, and quoted a spokesperson for the Machache Water Supply Movement saying that they host the project and that it is on their land.
fields_add.confidence_note: The P-number, the credit and grant numbers, the 2,798 affected households, the 183 outstanding compensation cases, the six households relocated, the ten fatalities, the 2012 blasting without permits and the involvement of the ombudsman all come from the World Bank's own completion report of 26 June 2019 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The review repeats the six households, the 2,615 of 2,798 compensated and the 550 female-headed households, but omits the ten fatalities, the blasting without permits, the uncontrolled blast of August 2012 and the ombudsman. The report gives no cause for any of the ten deaths and does not say when or where they happened or who the dead were, so none is counted here. The Bank's figures and the Metolong Authority's figures reported four months earlier do not match exactly: the report counts 2,798 affected households and 183 outstanding compensation cases at 31 December 2018, against the 2,786 affected families and 247 unpaid reported for August 2018. GroundUp's February 2026 report that the host communities still have no tap water is the independent account; it gives the dam's cost as R7 billion and names the World Bank among the lenders, and carries no figures on compensation or resettlement.
fields_add.killed_note: The World Bank's completion report of 26 June 2019 states that there were ten fatalities during implementation of the Metolong Dam and Water Supply Programme, and that all of them were properly reported and settled following the requirements of Lesotho's Labour Code. The sentence stands in the report's paragraph on the grievance redress mechanism. The report gives no cause, no date, no place and no identity for any of the ten, and settlement under the Labour Code is not a statement that the works caused the deaths, so none is counted. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the report omits the ten fatalities entirely.
